questions.q: What is the minimum number of degrees you must rotate a square to see it look exactly like it did at the start?
questions.a: The answer is 90°. If a student says 360°, they have forgotten that the square matches itself at quarter-turns; this reveals they are confusing "full rotation" with "rotational symmetry."

questions.q: If a shape has an order of rotational symmetry of 3, how many times does it look the same in one full 360° turn?
questions.a: It looks the same 3 times. A student answering "4" is likely including the 360° position as an "extra" count or confusing order with the number of sides, showing they haven't grasped that order is the total count of identical positions.

questions.q: A rectangle is rotated 180°. Does it look the same as it did at the start?
questions.a: Yes, it does. By mentally tracking the corners (e.g., top-left corner moving to bottom-right), the student can see the overlap; a "No" answer suggests the student is only looking at the outline and not the orientation of the sides.

questions.q: Compare a square and a regular hexagon. Which one has a higher order of rotational symmetry, and why?
questions.a: The hexagon has an order of 6, while the square has an order of 4; therefore, the hexagon is higher. A wrong answer suggests the student is counting lines of symmetry instead of rotational positions.

questions.q: Is it possible for a shape to have rotational symmetry but NOT line symmetry? Give an example.
questions.a: Yes, a parallelogram (that is not a rectangle) has rotational symmetry of order 2 but no lines of symmetry. Students who answer "No" believe that if a shape is symmetric in one way, it must be symmetric in all ways.

questions.q: Design a simple 2D figure that has rotational symmetry of order 2. Explain how you would verify this.
questions.a: A simple rectangle or a "Z" shape would work. The verification must involve tracing the shape, marking the center, and showing that rotating the tracing by 180° aligns perfectly with the original.
